items.definition: a trip from one place to another, especially a long one
exampleSentences: The journey from Paris to Rome took eight hours.
We had a long journey by train.

items.definition: a small piece of paper or a card that lets you travel or enter a place
exampleSentences: I bought a ticket for the six o'clock train.
Don't forget your plane ticket.

items.definition: the bags and suitcases you take with you when you travel
exampleSentences: My luggage was too heavy for the plane.
We put our luggage in the trunk of the taxi.

items.definition: an official document that shows who you are and lets you travel to other countries
exampleSentences: Remember to bring your passport to the airport.
Her passport is valid for ten more years.

items.definition: a time when something happens later than planned
exampleSentences: There was a two-hour delay at the airport.
Bad weather caused a delay in our flight.

items.definition: to reach the place you are traveling to
exampleSentences: We arrived at the hotel late at night.
What time does the train arrive in Boston?

items.definition: to leave a place, especially at the start of a trip
exampleSentences: Our flight departs at nine in the morning.
The bus departs from platform three.

items.definition: to arrange to have a seat, room, or ticket before you need it
exampleSentences: We booked our hotel room two months early.
I need to book a flight to Madrid.

items.definition: the raised area next to the train tracks where you wait for a train
exampleSentences: The train to Chicago leaves from platform two.
We waited on the platform for twenty minutes.

items.definition: a rectangular bag with a handle, used for carrying clothes when you travel
exampleSentences: I packed my suitcase the night before the trip.
Her suitcase was too big for the overhead bin.

items.definition: a place to stay, like a hotel or a guesthouse
exampleSentences: We found cheap accommodation near the beach.
The tour price includes accommodation and breakfast.

items.definition: to arrive at a hotel or an airport and tell the staff you are there, so you can get your room or your seat
exampleSentences: We checked in at the hotel at three o'clock.
You need to check in two hours before an international flight.
Can we check in early, or is the room not ready yet?

items.definition: in or to a foreign country
exampleSentences: She studied abroad for a year.
This is the first time we've traveled abroad.

items.definition: visiting the interesting places that tourists usually visit
exampleSentences: We spent our first day sightseeing in the old town.
Sightseeing all day made us very tired.

items.definition: something you buy on a trip to remember the place
exampleSentences: I bought a souvenir from every city I visited.
This small statue is a souvenir from our trip to Athens.

items.definition: belonging to or connected with the particular area or place you are in
exampleSentences: We asked a local for the best place to eat.
The local market sells fresh fruit every morning.

items.definition: a person who is visiting a place for pleasure, not for work
exampleSentences: The old city is full of tourists in the summer.
We didn't feel like tourists after living there for a month.

items.definition: a person who shows visitors around a place and gives them information
exampleSentences: Our guide told us the history of the castle.
We hired a guide for the mountain trip.

items.definition: the money that is used in a particular country
exampleSentences: You need to change your money into the local currency.
The currency in Japan is the yen.

items.definition: to change money from one currency into another
exampleSentences: We exchanged our dollars for euros at the airport.
Where can I exchange money near the hotel?

items.definition: the way you need to go to reach a place
exampleSentences: Could you give me directions to the train station?
We went in the wrong direction and got lost.

items.definition: the place where two streets meet
exampleSentences: The bank is on the corner of Main Street and Fifth Avenue.
Turn right at the next corner.

items.definition: a place where two or more roads meet or cross each other
exampleSentences: Turn left at the crossroads and you'll see the church.
There is a small cafe near the crossroads.

items.definition: an area of a city with streets on every side, like a square
exampleSentences: The museum is two blocks from here.
Walk three blocks and turn left.

items.definition: directly in front of you, without turning
exampleSentences: Go straight ahead until you reach the traffic light.
The hotel is straight ahead, next to the bank.

items.definition: a marked place on the road where people can safely walk across
exampleSentences: Always cross the street at the crosswalk.
There is a crosswalk in front of the school.

items.definition: a place where several roads meet in a circle
exampleSentences: Take the second exit at the roundabout.
There's a big roundabout before you reach the bridge.

items.definition: a sign at the side of a road that shows the way to a place
exampleSentences: Follow the signposts to the city center.
There was no signpost, so we got lost.

items.definition: unable to find your way or know where you are
exampleSentences: We got lost on our way to the hotel.
Don't worry if you get lost, just ask someone.

items.definition: not far away; close to a place
exampleSentences: There is a nearby cafe where we can wait.
Is there a pharmacy nearby?

lessons.title: Grammar: Past simple: regular and irregular verbs

items.headword: Past simple: regular and irregular verbs
items.definition: how to talk about trips and things that happened in the past
items.explanationTR:
We use the past simple to talk about actions that finished in the past, like a trip we took last year.

For regular verbs, add -ed to the base form: arrive becomes arrived, book becomes booked, stay becomes stayed. If the verb ends in -e, just add -d. If it ends in a consonant plus y, change y to i and add -ed: carry becomes carried. If there is a vowel before the y, just add -ed: stay becomes stayed.

Many common verbs are irregular, so they don't follow this rule. You have to learn their past forms: go becomes went, buy becomes bought, see becomes saw, take becomes took, get becomes got, have becomes had, leave becomes left, fly becomes flew.

• We arrived at the hotel at midnight.
• They flew to Lisbon last summer.
• I bought my ticket online.
• She didn't book a room, so we looked for one at the last minute.
• Did you see the old town?

For negative sentences, use didn't plus the base form: We didn't arrive on time. For questions, use Did plus the subject plus the base form: Did you enjoy the trip?

questions.prompt: We ---- at the airport two hours before our flight.
questions.explanationTR: The trip already happened, so we need the past simple: arrived. "Arrives" and "arriving" are not past forms, and "have arrive" is not a correct verb form.

questions.prompt: Last year, they ---- to Portugal for their vacation.
questions.explanationTR: Fly is irregular, and its past simple form is flew, not flied. "Flown" is the past participle, used with have, not by itself in the past simple.

questions.prompt: I ---- my ticket online last week.
questions.explanationTR: Buy is irregular, and its past simple form is bought. "Buyed" and "boughted" are not real words, and buy/buying are not past forms.

questions.prompt: We ---- a hotel room, so we slept at a friend's house.
questions.explanationTR: Negative past simple sentences use didn't plus the base form: didn't book. After didn't, the verb never takes -ed or -ing.

questions.prompt: ---- you enjoy your trip to Mexico?
questions.explanationTR: Past simple questions use Did + subject + base form: Did you enjoy...? "Do" and "Does" are present tense, and "Were" or "Have" would need a different verb form (enjoying, enjoyed).

questions.prompt: We ---- to the museum on our first day.
questions.explanationTR: Go is irregular, and its past simple form is went, not goed. "Gone" is the past participle, used with have, not alone in the past simple.

questions.prompt: She ---- a lot of photos during the trip.
questions.explanationTR: Take is irregular, and its past simple form is took. "Taken" is the past participle, used with have, and "taked" is not a real word.

questions.prompt: We ---- at a small guesthouse near the beach.
questions.explanationTR: Stay is a regular verb, so its past simple form simply adds -ed: stayed. "Staied" is a spelling mistake, since the y stays after a vowel.

items.definition: Short dialogues about finding places in a new town, with seven lines to complete

questions.prompt:
A: Excuse me, how do I get to the train station?
B: ----
A: Thank you very much!
options: It's two blocks away, on your left.
I don't really enjoy traveling by train very much.
The station was built more than one hundred years ago.
You should probably buy your ticket before you arrive.
Yes, I've been living in this city for many years.
questions.explanationTR: A asked how to get to the station, so the reply needs to give directions. The other replies talk about trains or the city in general but don't answer the question.

questions.prompt:
A: Is the museum far from here?
B: ----
A: Great, I'll walk then.
options: The museum usually closes early on Sunday afternoons.
No, it's just a five-minute walk.
I've actually never had the chance to visit it.
Yes, you could also take the number four bus there.
It's a very old building with a beautiful garden.
questions.explanationTR: A asks if the museum is far and then decides to walk, so B must have said it's close, like a five-minute walk. The other replies don't answer the distance question, and "Yes, you could take the bus" doesn't fit A's decision to walk.

questions.prompt:
A: Excuse me, I'm looking for the nearest pharmacy.
B: ----
A: Thanks! I'll go straight ahead.
options: The pharmacy is usually closed on Sunday afternoons.
I actually need to buy some medicine too, later today.
Go straight ahead and it's on the corner.
You can also pay for your medicine with a credit card.
It's much more expensive than the one near downtown.
questions.explanationTR: A repeats "straight ahead" in the next line, so B's reply must have given that direction. The other options mention pharmacies but don't say how to get there.

questions.prompt:
A: Could you tell me the way to the bank?
B: ----
A: Turn right, thanks a lot.
options: The bank usually opens at nine in the morning, I think.
You can pay for almost anything there in cash these days.
I believe the bank might be closed for a holiday today.
Sure, turn right at the corner and it's on your left.
I usually just walk to the bank when I need money.
questions.explanationTR: A confirms "turn right" in the next line, so B's reply must include that direction. The other replies are about the bank's hours or payments, not how to get there.

questions.prompt:
A: Excuse me, where's the nearest bus stop?
B: ----
A: Okay, I'll go now, thanks.
options: The bus around here comes about every ten minutes or so.
I don't really take the bus very often these days.
You will need exact change if you want to pay for the bus.
I heard the bus stop was moved somewhere last year.
It's just around the corner, next to the bakery.
questions.explanationTR: A asked where the bus stop is, so the reply must give its location, not how often the bus comes or how to pay for it. "Around the corner, next to the bakery" is the only reply that answers where.

questions.prompt:
A: I'm trying to find a supermarket near here. Can you help?
B: ----
A: Perfect, that's not far at all.
options: There's one two blocks down, on the right.
I usually just do most of my shopping online these days.
The supermarket is having a really big sale this week.
I'm not sure, I don't know where the exit is either.
You should probably bring a shopping list with you.
questions.explanationTR: A says the place isn't far, so B must have told them where it is, like "two blocks down, on the right." The other replies are about shopping habits or sales, not location.

questions.prompt:
A: Excuse me, how far is the hotel from here?
B: ----
A: Thanks, I think I can walk there.
options: The hotel actually has a really nice swimming pool.
It's about ten minutes on foot, down this street.
I actually stayed at that same hotel last summer.
You should probably book your room a bit in advance.
A taxi to the hotel can be quite expensive.
questions.explanationTR: A decides to walk after hearing the reply, so B must have said how far the hotel is and that it's walkable. The other replies talk about the hotel or taxis but don't answer how far it is.
